articles.title: They Saw It From the Mountain
articles.dek: Hebrews 11 lists the great heroes of faith and then says something surprising: none of them received what God promised. The reason it gives is one of the most hopeful sentences in the Bible.
articles.quote: God never meant his promise to be finished by one hero alone. He meant it to be finished by a family, and you belong to it.
articles.body:
On the night of April 3, 1968, a thunderstorm rolled over Memphis, Tennessee, and tornado warnings sounded across the city. Inside Mason Temple, a few thousand people had come out anyway. Many of them were the families of the city's sanitation workers, who had been on strike for weeks asking for safe equipment and a fair wage after two of their coworkers were crushed to death inside a garbage truck. Martin Luther King Jr. had stayed back at his motel that evening, exhausted and fighting a sore throat, and he sent his friend Ralph Abernathy to speak in his place. When Abernathy saw the crowd that had braved the storm, he phoned King and told him these people had come to hear him. King put on his coat and went.

He spoke largely without notes, with the wind banging the shutters of the old building. Near the end his voice rose, and he said words people still quote more than half a century later: "I just want to do God's will. And He's allowed me to go up to the mountain. And I've looked over. And I've seen the Promised Land. I may not get there with you. But I want you to know tonight, that we, as a people, will get to the Promised Land." The next evening he was shot on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel. He never walked into the future he described, yet the hope he spoke that night outlived him and was carried forward by people he would never meet.

King was borrowing a scene from the end of Deuteronomy. Moses, after forty years of leading a complaining nation through the desert, climbs Mount Nebo and looks across the Jordan. God shows him the whole land and says, "I have let you see it with your eyes, but you will not cross over into it" (Deuteronomy 34:4). It is one of the most tender and painful moments in Scripture. Centuries later, the writer of Hebrews built an entire chapter around that same experience, and he wrote it for people who badly needed it.

The letter to the Hebrews was written to Jewish believers in Jesus who were growing tired. Earlier in their faith they had stood their ground through public insult and had even "joyfully accepted the confiscation of [their] property" (Hebrews 10:34). Now the pressure was wearing them down, and some were tempted to slip back into a quieter, safer religion. So the writer opens a gallery of the faithful. He walks his readers past Abel, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses and Rahab, and then, as if he can feel the clock running out, he speeds up: "And what more shall I say? I do not have time to tell about Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah, about David and Samuel and the prophets" (Hebrews 11:32).

What follows reads like a montage of Israel's whole history. These people "shut the mouths of lions" (Hebrews 11:33), which any Jewish reader would recognize as Daniel's night in the den. They "quenched the fury of the flames" (Hebrews 11:34), the story of Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego walking unharmed in the furnace. "Women received back their dead, raised to life again" (Hebrews 11:35), recalling the widow of Zarephath and the woman of Shunem, whose sons were brought back to life through Elijah and Elisha (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 4). For a moment the chapter sounds like a list of victories, and a tired reader might wonder why his own life looks so different.

Then, halfway through the same verse, the music changes. "There were others who were tortured, refusing to be released so that they might gain an even better resurrection" (Hebrews 11:35). Many scholars hear in this an echo of a famous Jewish story from the second century BC, told in 2 Maccabees 7, in which a mother and her seven sons refused to abandon God's law under a foreign king and died speaking of the resurrection. The writer goes on: "They were put to death by stoning; they were sawed in two; they were killed by the sword" (Hebrews 11:37). An old Jewish tradition held that the prophet Isaiah died by being sawed in two under the wicked King Manasseh. Others wandered "in deserts and mountains, living in caves and in holes in the ground" (Hebrews 11:38), like the hundred prophets whom Obadiah hid in caves to save them from Queen Jezebel (1 Kings 18:4). In the middle of all this suffering the writer sets down a single line of judgment: "the world was not worthy of them" (Hebrews 11:38). The people the world treated as outcasts were, in God's eyes, too precious for the world that rejected them. Then he closes the whole chapter with this:

"These were all commended for their faith, yet none of them received what had been promised, since God had planned something better for us so that only together with us would they be made perfect." (Hebrews 11:39–40)

A chapter written to encourage people ends by admitting that none of its heroes received what God promised. The writer could have hidden that fact, and instead he puts it at the very end. He also tells us why. The word translated "commended" is the Greek martyrēthentes, from martyreō, "to bear witness" or "to testify." God himself testified on their behalf. Whatever the world said about the man in the cave or the woman who buried her sons, God took the witness stand and spoke well of them.

The second word is "perfect," from the Greek teleioō, which means to bring something to its finish or its intended goal. One way to read verse 40 is this: the heroes of faith are waiting at the finish line, and they will not cross it without the rest of the family. God "planned something better" (Hebrews 11:40), and "better" is a favorite word in Hebrews, used for the better hope and the better covenant that come through Jesus (Hebrews 7:19; 8:6). God's plan was always larger than any one life. Abraham, Moses and the unnamed prophets in the caves are part of a story that also includes the Hebrew believers who first read this letter, and it includes you. God never meant his promise to be finished by one hero alone. He meant it to be finished by a family, and you belong to it.

The very next sentence in the letter makes this personal: "Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses" (Hebrews 12:1). The word for "witnesses" there is martys, from the same root as "commended." The people God testified about now surround the runners still on the track. This suggests that heaven's grandstands are filled with people who care how your race goes, because your finish is bound up with theirs.

Filipinos understand this kind of faith better than most. Many of us are standing on the work of a lola who prayed every night for grandchildren she would not live to meet, or a father who spent twenty years abroad building a house he barely had time to sleep in. Some of you are doing that kind of work right now. You may be a teacher in a far barangay whose students will flourish long after you retire, or a parent sending money home and missing birthdays so that a child can finish school. Hebrews 11 tells you that this is the shape real faith has always taken, and that God sees and speaks well of it even when no one else does.

Today, think of one person who will come after you, perhaps a child, a student, or a younger coworker, and do one faithful thing for their future whose result you may never see. You might write a prayer for them in the front of a Bible, set aside a small amount for their schooling, or simply tell them what you have seen God do. If your own faithfulness feels invisible lately, remember that God has already taken the witness stand for people just like you.

Moses stood on Nebo and saw the land. A tired preacher in Memphis stood in a storm and said he had seen it too. You may be standing on a much smaller hill, but the view is the same, and the promise you are carrying will reach its finish together with all of God's people.

articles.title: The Friend Who Wouldn't Whitewash the Wall
articles.dek: Ezekiel faced prophets who told a frightened people only what they wanted to hear. Their soothing words did lasting damage, and the passage shows a better way to love the people closest to us.
articles.quote: The kindest people in your life are the ones who love you enough to show you where the wall is cracking, and who stay to help you rebuild it.
articles.body:
In late June 1940, during the most frightening summer of the Second World War, Clementine Churchill sat down at 10 Downing Street to write a letter to her husband. France had fallen only days before. Britain stood almost alone, and Winston, who had been prime minister for barely seven weeks, was carrying a weight few people in history have ever carried. Clementine loved him fiercely, and that love is the reason she could not stay silent about what she had been seeing.

"My Darling," she began, "I hope you will forgive me if I tell you something that I feel you ought to know." A devoted member of his staff had come to her privately, worried. Under the strain, Winston had become rough, sarcastic and overbearing with the people around him, so much so that some had stopped offering him their ideas. "I must confess that I have noticed a deterioration in your manner," she wrote, "and you are not so kind as you used to be." She gently reminded him that a man with his power needed the honest counsel of others, and that harshness would only leave him surrounded by frightened people. She signed it "Your loving devoted & watchful Clemmie," and beneath her name she drew a small cat. In a note at the end she admitted that she had written it the Sunday before and torn it up, "but here it is now."

That torn-up first draft tells us how hard it was to send. Telling him he was doing wonderfully would have been far easier, and in that terrible season almost anyone would have forgiven her for it. Clementine chose the harder kindness instead. The letter survives to this day, and it is one of the tenderest documents of the war, because it shows a woman who loved her husband too much to let him crumble behind a smooth surface.

Twenty-five centuries earlier, the prophet Ezekiel confronted people who had made the opposite choice. Ezekiel was a priest carried off to Babylon in 597 BC, along with King Jehoiachin and thousands of Jerusalem's leading families. Around 593 BC God called him to speak to the exiles living by the Kebar River. Jerusalem was still standing at the time, and a great many voices, both in Babylon and back home, were promising that the trouble would soon pass. Prophets rose up with comforting visions. The exile would be short, they said, the city was safe, and God was pleased with his people. Jeremiah, preaching in Jerusalem at the same time, heard the very same message and mourned that these leaders treated a deep wound "as though it were not serious" (Jeremiah 6:14).

In Ezekiel 13, God gives his prophet a picture from ordinary building work to describe what these smooth talkers were doing.

"Because they lead my people astray, saying, 'Peace,' when there is no peace, and because, when a flimsy wall is built, they cover it with whitewash, therefore tell those who cover it with whitewash that it is going to fall. Rain will come in torrents, and I will send hailstones hurtling down, and violent winds will burst forth." (Ezekiel 13:10–11)

Every listener by the Kebar River would have understood the image at once. Houses in that world were built of sun-dried mud brick, and a wall built carelessly could be made to look sturdy with a fresh coat of lime plaster. The Hebrew word for the flimsy wall, ḥayiṣ, appears only here in the Old Testament and seems to describe a thin partition, a wall of loosely stacked stones with nothing holding it together. The word for whitewash, tāpēl, carries the sense of something plastered on, a coating that looks clean and fresh from a distance. A wall like that could pass inspection on a dry afternoon. When the winter rains came, though, unbaked mud softened and the whole thing slumped to the ground. God's question in verse 12 is almost painfully human: "When the wall collapses, will people not ask you, 'Where is the whitewash you covered it with?'" (Ezekiel 13:12). The comforting words, so pleasant at the time, would be nowhere to be found when they were needed most.

The most surprising part of the chapter comes near the end. We tend to think of flattery as a harmless kind of sin, too much sugar and nothing worse. God, however, names two wounds these false prophets caused together: "Because you disheartened the righteous with your lies, when I had brought them no grief, and because you encouraged the wicked not to turn from their evil ways and so save their lives" (Ezekiel 13:22). One way to read this is that whitewashing gets love wrong in both directions at once. The people who were honestly trying to walk with God were made to feel burdened and condemned, while the people drifting toward ruin were assured that all was well. The flatterers handed out comfort and accusation to exactly the wrong people.

True love does the reverse. It lifts up the discouraged heart that God has not condemned, and it speaks honestly to the person heading toward a fall. Clementine did both in a single letter. She told Winston the hard truth about his manner, and she wrapped it in such obvious devotion that he could not mistake her motive. She wanted him strong, and she wanted him to finish well. Proverbs puts it simply: "Wounds from a friend can be trusted, but an enemy multiplies kisses" (Proverbs 27:6). Paul gives the same balance in a single phrase, urging believers to grow up into Christ by "speaking the truth in love" (Ephesians 4:15).

For many Filipinos, this is tender ground. We are a people who value pakikisama, the grace of getting along, and we feel hiya keenly, that deep reluctance to embarrass someone or disturb the peace. These are beautiful instincts, and they hold families and barangays together. Yet they can slowly turn into whitewash. We say "okay lang 'yan" to a cousin whose gambling is draining the household, or keep smiling at a friend whose marriage is quietly cracking, because speaking up feels rude. We tell ourselves we are keeping the peace, when in fact we are only plastering a wall we can already see is leaning.

Ezekiel's answer is neither harshness nor bluntness for its own sake. The false prophets were condemned for lying, and a harsh word can be just as false as a flattering one. The better path is the one Clementine walked: honest words, spoken privately, with humility and obvious affection, by someone who intends to stay. She did not shame her husband in public or write him off. She wrote as his wife, someone who would still be beside him the next morning. That is the posture that makes truth bearable, and it is the posture God himself takes throughout Ezekiel, whose hardest warnings are always aimed at bringing his people home (Ezekiel 14:11).

The passage also invites us to welcome the honest people in our own lives. Churchill could easily have resented his wife's letter. Many of his biographers believe he took it to heart, and the two remained devoted to each other for the rest of their long marriage. It takes humility to say, "Tell me the truth, even when it stings," and it is one of the surest ways to keep your own walls from becoming plaster over mud.

So think of one person you love whose wall you have watched beginning to crack. Before you say anything, pray for them, and ask God to give you both courage and gentleness. Then, perhaps this week, find a quiet moment to speak honestly, and let your affection be as plain as your words. And if someone has already done that for you, thank them, because they took a risk for your sake. The kindest people in your life are the ones who love you enough to show you where the wall is cracking, and who stay to help you rebuild it. May God make you that kind of friend, and give you a few of them too.

articles.title: Light Enough for the Next Step
articles.dek: The most beloved verse in Psalm 119 was written at night, by a man holding his life in his hands. That is why its small lamp is such good news for anyone walking in the dark.
articles.quote: God's word is a lamp held low, close to your feet, and its light is exactly enough for the next faithful step.
articles.body:
In the warm waters of the Indo-Pacific, including reefs around the Philippines, lives a small dark fish that carries its own lamp. The splitfin flashlight fish spends its days tucked inside caves and crevices, and on moonless nights it rises toward the open reef to feed. Beneath each eye sits a bean-shaped pouch that glows a soft blue-green. That glow belongs to someone else: the pouch is packed with living bacteria that shine continuously, and the fish keeps them alive by supplying them through its own blood, giving them shelter and food in exchange for their light.

Marine biologists who studied these fish in darkened tanks found that they use the light much as we would use a flashlight. It reaches only a short distance, enough to spot the tiny plankton they eat and to keep track of companions swimming nearby. When the fish wants to go dark, it can rotate the organ down into a pocket of black skin, and the light winks out until it turns it back up again. A fish that could see the whole reef would have no need of such equipment. This one sees a little at a time, and that small, close light has been enough to carry its kind through the darkness of the sea for a very long time.

Filipinos who grew up with brownouts understand this better than most. Many of us remember doing homework beside a gasera, the little kerosene lamp that threw a circle of yellow light just wide enough for one notebook, or walking through the house at night holding a candle that lit the floor in front of us and very little else. The gasera lit the page, and the page was all you needed to finish the lesson.

Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, 176 verses arranged as an acrostic, a poem in which each section begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. There are twenty-two stanzas of eight lines each, and in the original every line within a stanza starts with the same letter. Today's stanza, verses 105 to 112, belongs to the letter nun. The poet never gives his name, and across the whole psalm he talks to God about one subject only: God's word, which he calls by many names, including law, statutes, precepts, decrees and commands. It reads like a long love letter written by someone who has found the one thing he cannot live without.

This stanza opens with the line many Christians learned as children, and then, almost immediately, the poet tells us where he is standing when he writes it. “I have suffered much,” he says; “preserve my life, LORD, according to your word” (Psalm 119:107). Two lines later he adds, “Though I constantly take my life in my hands, I will not forget your law” (Psalm 119:109), and then, “The wicked have set a snare for me, but I have not strayed from your precepts” (Psalm 119:110). The first line of the stanza was written by a man in danger, on a dark road, with enemies hiding traps along the way.

“Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path.” (Psalm 119:105)

The word for lamp here is the Hebrew ner. In ancient Israel a ner was a small clay saucer about the size of a palm, filled with olive oil, its rim pinched at one side to hold a wick of flax or linen. Archaeologists have uncovered thousands of them in houses and tombs throughout the land. Its flame gave off about as much light as a single candle. Carried on a night road and held low, it showed the ground a step or two ahead: where to set your foot, whether a stone or a hole or a snake lay in the way. The poet chose his words with care when he wrote “a lamp for my feet.” He was asking God for footing, for the next safe place to step.

Verse 109 deepens the picture. The phrase the NIV renders “I constantly take my life in my hands” reads literally, “My soul is in my palm continually.” It was a Hebrew way of describing someone fully exposed to danger. Jephthah used it when he went out alone against the Ammonites: “I took my life in my hands” (Judges 12:3). Jonathan used it of the young David walking out to face Goliath: “He took his life in his hands when he killed the Philistine” (1 Samuel 19:5). One way to read this stanza is to picture the psalmist with both hands full. In one palm he holds his own fragile life, exposed and easily spilled. In the other he holds a small clay lamp. He cannot see the end of the road, and he cannot see who is hiding along it, yet he can see the ground under his next step, and in the dark that is what keeps a person alive.

That is also why the snare in verse 110 matters. Hunters in the ancient world set nets and nooses along the paths animals used, hidden under leaves where nothing in daylight would give them away. A traveler at night would walk right into one. The lamp held near the feet is the very thing that reveals the trap before the foot comes down. When the psalmist says, “I have not strayed from your precepts,” he is describing a man who kept his light close to the ground.

Then, in the middle of all this danger, he says something that sounds almost cheerful: “Your statutes are my heritage forever; they are the joy of my heart” (Psalm 119:111). The word for heritage is nachalah, the word Israel used for the family land each tribe received in Canaan. It meant security, a home, something to pass on to your children. The priests were given no land at all, and God told them, “I am your share and your inheritance among the Israelites” (Numbers 18:20). This suggests the psalmist may have felt he had lost much of what others counted as security, and so he made the same discovery the priests were meant to make. What God had spoken was land he could stand on, and no enemy could take it from him.

The rest of Scripture keeps returning to this image. Proverbs says, “For this command is a lamp, this teaching is a light” (Proverbs 6:23). Peter, writing near the end of his life, told believers to pay attention to God's word “as to a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Peter 1:19). The promise has always been for people who are still walking before sunrise.

Most of us, if we are honest, would rather have a floodlight. We want God to show us the next five years: whether the contract abroad will be renewed, whether the test results will be good, whether the child who has wandered will come home, whether the business will survive the year. God's word is a lamp held low, close to your feet, and its light is exactly enough for the next faithful step. It will usually show you what to do this morning: forgive this person, tell the truth in this conversation, rest instead of worrying, pray before you answer that message. Then, tomorrow, it will show you the step after that.

The little flashlight fish keeps its glow by keeping its partners close and fed, and the psalmist kept his lamp burning in a similar way. He had “taken an oath and confirmed it” (Psalm 119:106), and he closes the stanza with, “My heart is set on keeping your decrees to the very end” (Psalm 119:112). His light stayed bright because he stayed near the source of it, day after day, without waiting to feel safe first.

Tonight, before you sleep, you might copy verse 105 onto a small card or into your phone and ask God one simple question with it: what is the next step this word shows me for tomorrow? You do not need to see the whole road to walk it well. Keep the lamp near your feet, take the step it shows you, and trust the One who holds the road, the night, and your life in his own hands.

articles.title: The Joy on the Other Side of Instruction
articles.dek: A father in Proverbs says his very kidneys will rejoice when his child speaks wisely. Behind that strange phrase is a picture of how God himself feels about the people he trains.
articles.quote: Every correction God gives you comes from a Father who is already leaning forward, waiting for the day his heart can be glad over you.
articles.body:
In 2001, Google was a young, fast-growing company with two brilliant founders and a newly hired chief executive named Eric Schmidt. Schmidt had already run a large technology firm, and when the board suggested he meet regularly with a coach, he later admitted that his first reaction was that he did not need one. The coach was Bill Campbell, a former college football coach from Columbia University who had gone on to lead the software company Intuit and to advise Steve Jobs at Apple. Schmidt agreed to the meetings anyway, and they continued for some fifteen years. By the end, he described Campbell as one of the most important people in the company's history.

After Campbell died in 2016, Schmidt and two fellow Google executives, Jonathan Rosenberg and Alan Eagle, interviewed dozens of the people he had coached and wrote a book about him called Trillion Dollar Coach. What they found surprised them. Campbell could be blunt to the point of embarrassment, and he told powerful people hard truths they did not want to hear. Yet the people he corrected loved him, because they could see that his deepest satisfaction came from watching them grow. On weekends this man who advised billionaires also coached a youth flag football team at a local school, and when he died, hundreds of people gathered on that school's football field to say goodbye. His joy had always been in his players.

That same kind of joy sits at the heart of today's reading. Proverbs 23 belongs to a section often called the "sayings of the wise" (Proverbs 22:17 to 24:22), a collection of short teachings framed as a parent or teacher speaking to a young person about to step into adult life. The setting is a household, possibly a royal court where young officials were trained, and the voice is tender and urgent at once. The teacher begins by calling the young person to pay attention, then speaks frankly about correcting children, and finally opens his heart about what he hopes to see.

Verse 12 begins with a call: "Apply your heart to instruction and your ears to words of knowledge" (Proverbs 23:12). The Hebrew verb behind "apply" literally means "bring." The student is asked to carry his heart into the classroom, to show up with his whole self instead of just sitting in the room. Then the teacher turns to parents in verses 13 and 14, saying that discipline will not destroy a child and will in fact "save them from death" (Proverbs 23:14). The Hebrew word for "discipline" in verse 13 is musar, and it is the very same word translated "instruction" in verse 12. One way to read this is that the correction we received as children and the instruction we are asked to welcome as adults are one continuous gift. The teacher's goal throughout is rescue, keeping a young life away from the paths that lead to ruin.

Then the voice softens, and the teacher lets us see what all the correcting has been for.

"My son, if your heart is wise, then my heart will be glad indeed; my inmost being will rejoice when your lips speak what is right." (Proverbs 23:15–16)

The phrase "my inmost being" translates the Hebrew word kilyotay, which literally means "my kidneys." In ancient Israel the kidneys were thought of as the hidden seat of a person's deepest feelings, the place where emotion lived beneath the surface. The verb "rejoice" here is a strong one, often used for exulting or celebrating. So the father is saying that when his child speaks with wisdom, the joy will reach the most private part of him. The words "what is right" come from mesharim, a word that carries the sense of straightness or evenness, like a path that has been leveled. He is picturing a day when his child's words run straight and true.

Read in that light, the whole passage becomes a love letter. The call to listen in verse 12 and the hard words about discipline in verses 13 and 14 make sense once you reach verses 15 and 16, because the teacher has shown his motive. He corrects because he is longing for the moment his heart can be glad. Bill Campbell's players could take his bluntness because they knew what he wanted for them, and the young person in Proverbs is invited to receive correction in that same spirit.

This is where the passage opens onto the gospel, the good news of what God has done for us in Jesus. The rest of Scripture describes God as exactly this kind of Father. Hebrews quotes Proverbs directly: "the Lord disciplines the one he loves" (Hebrews 12:6), and then adds an honest admission, "No discipline seems pleasant at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it produces a harvest of righteousness and peace for those who have been trained by it" (Hebrews 12:11). The prophet Zephaniah pictures God's own heart rising with the same gladness as the father in Proverbs: "He will take great delight in you; in his love he will no longer rebuke you, but will rejoice over you with singing" (Zephaniah 3:17).

The order matters here. In the gospel, God's love comes first and his training follows. Before Jesus preached a sermon or performed a miracle, his Father spoke from heaven at his baptism: "This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased" (Matthew 3:17). Through faith in Christ, believers are brought into that same family and that same love. God does not train you in order to decide whether he will love you. He trains you because you already belong to him, and every correction God gives you comes from a Father who is already leaning forward, waiting for the day his heart can be glad over you.

That changes how we can receive the uncomfortable moments of life. Many of us grew up associating correction with shame, perhaps from a stern parent, a harsh teacher, or a boss who seemed to enjoy pointing out mistakes. So when a friend tells us a hard truth, or when Scripture presses on a habit we would rather keep, we brace ourselves as though we were about to be rejected. Proverbs 23 invites a different posture, because it lets us hear the warmth behind the instruction. The conviction you feel when you snap at your spouse, the nudge to apologize to a coworker, the verse that keeps coming back to you about your spending, can all be received as the voice of a Father who wants to rejoice over you.

It also gives a model for those of us who correct others. Parents, teachers, managers, and church leaders carry real authority, and the passage reminds us that the aim of correction is the other person's flourishing. Campbell's players trusted him because his delight in them was obvious. If the people under your care rarely see your joy in them, your correction will feel like judgment, however accurate it may be. A good practice is to let them hear your gladness as clearly as they hear your instruction, telling a child or a colleague specifically when their words were wise and kind.

Today, when some word of correction reaches you, whether through Scripture, a friend, or your own conscience, you might pause and pray a simple sentence: "Father, I bring you my heart; teach me, because I know you love me." That is what verse 12 means by bringing your heart to instruction. And somewhere in the quiet of that prayer, you can picture the Father of Proverbs 23 and of Zephaniah 3, leaning in with a glad heart, rejoicing over you as you walk his straight path.
